entities.name: Andrea dei Mozzi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Andrea dei Mozzi, an Italian bishop from the powerful Florentine Mozzi banking family, navigated the complex ecclesiastical and political landscape of the late 13th century, ultimately achieving the prestigious Archbishopric of Florence before a scandalous transfer immortalized him in literary history. His career, spanning from papal chaplaincies under Popes Alexander IV and Gregory IX, culminated in his appointment as Archbishop of Florence in 1287, a position of immense spiritual and temporal influence within the Tuscan heartland.

Mozzi's tenure in Florence was marked by a decline in reputation, leading Pope Boniface VIII to transfer him to the less significant See of Vicenza in 1295. This abrupt reassignment, widely perceived as a demotion due to alleged impropriety or incompetence, became a significant ecclesiastical scandal of the era. He died shortly after his transfer in 1296, his brief and controversial episcopate in Vicenza sealing his fate in contemporary opinion.

The most enduring consequence of Andrea dei Mozzi's life and scandal was his unexpected and damning inclusion in Dante Alighieri's *The Inferno*. Dante, a contemporary Florentine, condemned Mozzi to the third bolgia of the eighth circle of Hell, reserved for simoniacs, though some interpretations suggest his placement relates to other moral failings. This literary judgment cemented his image as a figure of clerical corruption and ensured his remembrance far beyond the typical scope of a medieval bishop.

Thus, a man whose ecclesiastical career ended in disgrace gained an unforeseen and eternal, if ignominious, fame through the pen of Italy's greatest poet; a divine comedy of errors transformed into a permanent fixture of infernal punishment.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andrea dei Mozzi's significance primarily stems from his controversial transfer from Florence and subsequent immortalization in Dante Alighieri's *The Inferno*, ensuring his lasting, albeit infamous, place in cultural memory. His story offers a specific window into late 13th-century ecclesiastical politics and moral perceptions within the Church.
